How to Write an Ideal Customer Profile Sales Will Use

Playbooklowob research

By Chris WellsFrom lowob RESEARCH · 13 May 2026 · 8-minute read · Strategy

An ideal customer profile (ICP) is a written description of the customer a company should pursue first: the one most likely to buy, most likely to succeed with the product, and most likely to stay. It should tell sales whom to pursue, why a company fits, and when to move on. A working ICP has five parts: firmographic facts, situational triggers, the buying committee, disqualifiers and the evidence it was built from. If every prospect qualifies, it is not an ICP.

An ideal customer profile (ICP) is a written description of the customer a company should pursue first: the one most likely to buy, most likely to succeed with the product, and most likely to stay. It is the practical output of positioning, and it is the document that keeps marketing and sales pointed at the same people.

Most ICPs are written once, put in a slide, and ignored, because they describe a customer so broadly that every prospect qualifies.

What an ICP contains

Firmographic or demographic facts. For business buyers: industry, size, geography, stage, structure. For consumers: age, situation, income band, location. These are the filters, and they are the least interesting part.

Situational triggers. What is happening to the customer that makes the problem urgent now: a new regulation, a product launch, a failed vendor, a new leader, a funding event, a growth spurt, a deadline. Triggers explain why two identical companies buy at different times, and they are what makes an ICP useful for outbound.

The buying committee. Who feels the problem, who approves the spend, who can block it, and who has to implement. For consumer products, who influences the decision.

Disqualifiers. The characteristics that predict a bad customer: too small to pay, a technical stack the product does not fit, a use case it does not serve, a regulatory position the company cannot support. The disqualifier list is usually more valuable than the qualifier list, because it stops the pipeline filling with deals that will not close or will churn.

Evidence. The customers this description was built from, and what happened to them.

ComponentWhat to writeIllustrative entryWhere the evidence comes from
FirmographicsIndustry, size, geography, stageRegulated lenders, 200 to 2,000 staff, USCRM fields on won deals
TriggersThe event that makes it urgent nowNew disclosure rule due within two quartersDiscovery notes on the last ten wins
Buying committeeWho feels, approves, blocks, implementsCompliance lead feels it; CFO approves; IT security can blockContacts engaged on won and lost deals
DisqualifiersWhat predicts a bad customerNo in-house compliance owner; legacy core system the product cannot connect toChurned accounts and lost deals
EvidenceThe customers it was built fromNamed internally, with outcome for eachRetention and expansion data

The buying committee row is longer than most teams write it. Forrester's State of Business Buying 2024 found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, and 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. Our explainer What is a buying committee? covers the roles to record.

ICP versus persona

An ICP describes the account or the customer: the company or person worth pursuing. A persona describes an individual within the buying process: their role, goals, fears, and how they evaluate. A company sells to an ICP and communicates with personas. Confusing the two produces marketing aimed at "the CFO" with no view on which CFOs, at which companies, in which situation.

Ideal customer profilePersona
DescribesThe account worth pursuingA person inside the buying process
AnswersShould we pursue this company, now?What does this person need to believe, and how do they evaluate?
Built fromWon, lost and churned accountsInterviews and call recordings
Used bySales for qualification, marketing for targeting, outbound for listsMarketing for messaging, sales for call preparation
Fails whenEvery prospect qualifiesIt is written without an ICP behind it

The distinction matters for measurement. Forrester's analyst Simon Daniels wrote in 2023 that fewer than 1% of leads convert to closed deals, partly because several leads contribute to one opportunity. Forrester clients reported a 50% increase in meeting-to-closed-won conversion when marketing delivered three or more members of the buying group to sales. An ICP tells you which accounts; personas tell you which people in them to reach.

How to build one from evidence

Start with the customers who bought fastest, paid the most, expanded, and stayed. Pull their characteristics, the trigger that made them buy, who was involved, and what they said the problem was. Do the same for customers who churned or deals that were lost, and record what distinguished them. The pattern across both sets is the ICP. The differences are the disqualifiers.

This is also the raw material of positioning. April Dunford's method counts best-fit customers as one of the five components of a position, and starts from competitive alternatives: what those customers would do if the product did not exist. An ICP and a position built from the same customer set will agree with each other.

Size and logo appeal are poor substitutes for that evidence. Gartner research reported by CRM Magazine in December 2021 found 58% of B2B sales organisations missed quota on key accounts, and that customers elevated to key-account status mainly because of their large spend were 51% less likely to increase it over time. The largest account is not always the best fit.

Sales benchmarks point the same way. Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 analysis of 4.2 million opportunities at 530 companies, which is vendor research, found top performers prioritised the kinds of accounts and personas they had closed before and disqualified poor-fit opportunities early. Successful deals engaged about nine contacts by the solution-presented stage, against about two for lost deals.

If the company has fewer than ten customers, the ICP is a hypothesis, and it should say so. Write it narrowly anyway; a narrow hypothesis can be tested, and a broad one cannot. Our piece on segment selection with evidence shows how to score segments on win rate, deal size, cycle length and retention once the data exists.

A narrow hypothesis can be tested, and a broad one cannot.

The mistakes that make it useless

Five mistakes account for most ICPs that nobody uses.

  1. Writing it broadly so nobody is excluded.
  2. Building it from who the company wishes it sold to rather than who actually bought.
  3. Leaving out triggers, so it cannot inform timing.
  4. Leaving out disqualifiers, so it cannot inform saying no.
  5. Writing it once and never revising it as the customer base changes.

The fifth is the slowest to show. A profile built from the first ten customers often describes early adopters, who tolerate gaps that the next fifty will not. Revisit it each quarter against the accounts won, lost and churned since the last version.

How to tell whether it is working

An ICP is working when four things are true. Sales can disqualify a lead in one call using shared criteria. Marketing can describe the audience for a channel test in the ICP's terms. Outbound lists are built from the triggers, not from a title search. And the customers acquired this quarter look more like the profile than the ones acquired last quarter.

An ICP that does those four things is a working document. One that does not is a slide. The next step is to turn it into a list of named accounts with owners, which Market maps that sales actually uses covers, and into outbound built on triggers, covered in Cold outreach works better with a real reason to talk.

lowob takeaways

  • Use real customer outcomes and buying signals to define fit. Build from who bought, paid, expanded and stayed, not who you wish you sold to.
  • Include reasons to disqualify an account. The disqualifier list stops the pipeline filling with deals that will not close or will churn.
  • Write the triggers. They make the ICP useful for timing and for outbound.
  • Check that marketing and sales use the same criteria. One profile, used to qualify, target and build lists.

Common questions

What should an ideal customer profile include?

Firmographic or demographic facts, the situational triggers that make the problem urgent, the buying committee, disqualifiers, and the evidence: the customers it was built from and what happened to them.

What is the difference between an ICP and a buyer persona?

An ICP describes the account worth pursuing. A persona describes a person inside the buying process, their role, goals and how they evaluate. A company sells to an ICP and communicates with personas.

How do you build an ICP with few customers?

Treat it as a hypothesis and say so. Write it narrowly from the customers you have, including why they bought and who was involved, and test it against the next deals.

How often should an ICP be updated?

Review it each quarter against the accounts won, lost and churned since the last version, and revise it when the customers being acquired stop matching it.
